buyback.source: FY2025 10-K: $89.3B repurchased (~2.4% of shares/yr); new $100B authorization approved Apr 30, 2026.
buyback.note: Apple retires ~2.4% of its shares a year. The probability-weighted fair value above divides by *today's* share count and already prices the cash Apple spends on buybacks (it sits in the FCFF stream). Shrinking the denominator as shares retire shows the per-share concentration continuing holders enjoy — but it is genuinely value-additive only when repurchases happen *below* intrinsic value. With the market above our intrinsic, the buybacks are technically dilutive to per-share value, so treat these buyback-adjusted figures as an illustrative upper bound, not the fair value.

wacc_sensitivity.note: Because ~75% of the value sits in the terminal value, the discount rate is the largest single swing factor. Our scenarios use a CAPM build-up with a ~50bp quality/buyback premium (Base ~8.4%). The sell-side 'quality compounder' camp applies ~7–7.5%; at those rates the weighted value re-rates toward the market — which is the crux of the whole valuation debate.

consensus.label: Street consensus (FY26–FY28), same engine
consensus.source: S&P Global / Visible Alpha aggregate of ~38–41 analysts (Jul 2026): FY26 revenue ~$478B (+15%), FY27 ~$522B, FY28 ~$562B; EPS $8.76 / $9.69 / $10.91.
consensus.note: The Street's own consensus revenue path, run through this same FCFF engine at the Base-case discount rate. It lands below our probability-weighted value because consensus EPS grows faster than revenue mainly through buybacks (~2.4%/yr fewer shares) — which a whole-firm DCF does not capture — with only mild operating-margin expansion. So even the analysts' explicit forecast implies an intrinsic well under the market price; the rest is multiple re-rating.

input.parts_intro: CuriosityStream reports one segment, but it runs three economically different streams, and the 10-Q discloses enough to separate them. A slowly shrinking subscription business. A licensing business that is genuinely growing. And, sitting inside that licensing line, a large and fast-growing block of trade-and-barter revenue — content swapped for content, on which no cash ever changes hands. Averaging those into one multiple would bury the only question that matters.
input.figures_intro: Each part's expected FY2027 figure times the multiple that stream deserves on its own merits. The barter block is carried at nil in the bear and base cases: it is real revenue under GAAP, it is not cash, and it cannot pay a dividend.
input.fundamentals_source: Segment splits and the barter block are as reported in the Q2 2026 10-Q (filed 13 Aug 2026) and the FY2025 10-K; the FY2027 figures are our own estimates, extrapolated from those disclosures and management's FY2026 guidance of $77–82M revenue.

parts.name: Subscription, bundled distribution & advertising
parts.note: Direct-to-consumer is in structural decline ($31.3M in FY2024 → $23.8M in FY2025); partner/bundled distribution is growing but not fast enough to offset it. Management says outright it is running this for durable economics rather than growth. Includes the small advertising and sponsorship line.

parts.name: Content & data licensing — cash
parts.note: Traditional factual-video licensing plus the AI training datasets and the 880-billion-token code corpus — the part of the licensing line that actually settles in cash. This single number decides the valuation.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.comment: The 2025–26 data-licensing burst was a one-off sale of a back catalogue, not a business. Buyers who have bought the corpus do not buy it twice; cash licensing falls back toward its pre-boom run rate and the multiple compresses to a library multiple.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.comment: Cash licensing keeps growing, but at the pace the cash line has actually shown rather than the pace the headline suggests: roughly $25M in FY2026 to $27M in FY2027. Subscription erodes a few percent. Barter keeps inflating reported revenue and is worth nothing.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.comment: The 17 productised datasets and the code corpus turn out to be a repeatable franchise with a renewing customer base rather than a catalogue clearance — cash licensing compounds to $42M and earns a data-licensor multiple. Some of the barter is genuinely convertible into cash later.

market.commentary: The price is not an input to anything above. Read the other way: crediting the subscription business and the cash at our own figures, the market is paying roughly 7.4× FY2027 cash licensing revenue — or, at our 2.5×, it is assuming about $80M of cash licensing revenue against our $27M. Cash licensing in the first half of 2026 was $10.9M, down from $11.3M a year earlier. Getting to $80M is not an extrapolation of that line; it is a different business.

A licensing business whose reported growth is almost entirely two things that are not recurring cash: a large block of trade-and-barter revenue, content swapped for content on which no money changes hands, and — new this quarter — an $8.5M licence sold to the buyer of three divested brands, collected in instalments from 2027. Averaging those into one multiple would bury the only question that matters.

Barter is carried at nil in the bear and base cases: it is real revenue under GAAP, it is not cash, and it cannot pay a dividend. The Curiosity Brands licence is not a part at all — it is a fixed receivable already sitting on the balance sheet, so it is carried in the bridge at its filed present value rather than capitalised at a revenue multiple.
input.fundamentals_source: Segment splits, the barter block, the Curiosity Brands licence (Note 16) and the Citibank revolver are as reported in the Q2 2026 10-Q (filed 13 Aug 2026); prior-year figures from the FY2025 10-K. The FY2027 figures are our own estimates, extrapolated from those disclosures and management's raised FY2026 guidance of $77–82M revenue.

parts.note: Direct-to-consumer is in structural decline ($31.3M in FY2024 → $23.8M in FY2025); partner/bundled distribution is growing but not fast enough to offset it. Management says outright it is running this for durable economics rather than growth. Includes the small advertising and sponsorship line, and from 1 July 2026 the consolidation of Spiegel Venture.

Excludes barter, and excludes the one-off Curiosity Brands licence. This single number decides the valuation.

adjustments.comment: The $10M licence sold on 30 June 2026, receivable as four annual instalments of $2.5M from June 2027 and booked at a 7% discount. Contracted cash, so it belongs in the bridge — but it is a fixed asset already earned, not a revenue stream, and capitalising it at a sales multiple as well would count it twice.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.comment: The 2025–26 data-licensing burst was a one-off sale of a back catalogue, not a business, and the first half of 2026 is what that looks like once barter and the disposal licence are stripped out. Buyers who have bought the corpus do not buy it twice; recurring cash licensing settles near its traditional-library level and the multiple compresses to a library multiple. The Curiosity Brands instalments are haircut for a counterparty that paid $0.3M for the brands and owes $10M for the licence.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.comment: Management delivers part of the second-half ramp its guidance requires but not all of it: recurring cash licensing recovers from a $2.4M first half to roughly $10M in FY2026 and $12M in FY2027, which is well above the current run rate and well below the headline. Subscription erodes a few percent. Barter keeps inflating reported revenue and is worth nothing.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.comment: The 880-billion-token code corpus and the productised datasets turn out to be a repeatable franchise with a renewing customer base rather than a catalogue clearance — recurring cash licensing compounds to $22M and earns a data-licensor multiple. Some of the barter is genuinely convertible into cash later.

market.commentary: The price is not an input to anything above. Read the other way: crediting the subscription business, the licence receivable and the cash at our own figures, the market is paying roughly 14× FY2027 recurring cash licensing revenue — or, at our 2.5×, it is assuming about $66M of it against our $12M. Recurring cash licensing in the first half of 2026, once barter and the Curiosity Brands licence are removed, was $2.4M, down from $11.3M a year earlier. Getting to $66M is not an extrapolation of that line; it is a different business. The stock fell 11% on 14 August, the day after the 10-Q disclosed what the 12 August earnings release did not.

action.rationale: The crux driver reads very weak evidence: the line the valuation turns on shrank 79% year on year once the two non-recurring blocks are removed, and its multiple spans 1.5× to 5.0×, which alone moves the answer four-fold. The notes still call the scenario weights the weakest input in the report. So the accumulate level is the bear case itself, not a discount to a weighted value those weights produced.
action.review: Second-half recurring cash licensing — reported licensing less barter, less the Curiosity Brands instalments — turns up against the prior year, or contracted backlog starts to carry the recurring revenue management describes.

input.history_intro: FormFactor's filed results, run through the same bridge this report uses for the future. Gross margin sat in a 39.0–41.9% band for nine consecutive years, and operating income was no higher in 2025 than in 2017 despite 43% more revenue. Then Q2 FY2026 printed 50.7%. Everything below turns on whether that line is a new floor or a cycle peak.
input.bridge_intro: No earnings figure is assumed. Each case names a revenue level, a gross margin and a dollar cost base, and the earnings fall out. That ordering is deliberate: with roughly $290M of largely fixed operating cost against $450–700M of gross profit, a few points of gross margin is the entire valuation, and stating EPS directly would bury the one assumption that matters.
input.figures_source: Balance sheet, share count and every history row are FormFactor's own filed figures (10-Q for the quarter ended June 27 2026; 10-K for FY2017–FY2025). The FY2027 revenue, margin and cost lines are this report's estimates, not company guidance — FormFactor guides one quarter at a time and has guided Q3 FY2026 to $270M ± $10M.

history.note: GAAP operating income was $82.8M; $73.0M of that was a gain on sale of business booked inside operating income. The bridge excludes it.
GAAP operating income was $64.8M, including a $20.6M gain on sale of business. Excluded here.
Opex includes $3.0M of factory start-up cost. No divestiture gain this year.
Quarter annualized. Gross margin was held down by $23.9M of unallocated cost of revenues, including acquisition fixed-asset step-up.
Quarter annualized. Unallocated cost of revenues fell to $6.7M. Probe Cards segment gross margin 54.4%, against 38.3% a year earlier.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.comment: HBM4 buildout digests and probe-card pricing normalizes as Micronics Japan and Technoprobe compete for the same sockets. Revenue falls 8% from FY2026 — smaller than the 11% drop FormFactor took in 2023 — and gross margin gives back most of the step-up to 42%, still above any year before 2026. Opex is held flat. The multiple compresses to 18× as the cycle turns.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.comment: The step-up is real but not fully durable. HBM probe cards carry a structurally richer margin than foundry and logic, and DRAM keeps gaining mix, but 48% sits below Q2's 50.7% because that quarter carried unusually low unallocated cost. Revenue grows 11% on HBM4 plus the co-packaged-optics ramp. 26× is roughly where large semi-test peers trade.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.comment: Test intensity re-rates the business permanently: HBM4 stacks need far more probe contact, co-packaged optics opens a second socket, and FormFactor holds share in both. Revenue grows 30% and Q2's margin proves a floor rather than a peak, giving a 29% operating margin — more than double anything in the filed record. A scarce-asset multiple of 34× follows.

market.commentary: The price is not asking for the base case with a better multiple — it is asking for a gross margin no test company has earned, or a revenue base 62% above the base case, or both in combination. That is the honest shape of the disagreement, and it is why this report ends well below the quote rather than near it.

action.rationale: The cases run from $23 to $145 — a six-fold spread off one assumption, the gross margin, with two quarters of evidence on one side and nine years on the other. When the weights are doing that much of the work, a fraction of the weighted value is not a real margin of safety, so the accumulate level is the Bear case itself: the price at which the model still holds if the margin reverts most of the way. The trim level is a plain 1.4× of fair value.
action.review: Two prints would settle it. If Probe Cards segment gross margin holds above 50% for two more quarters while DRAM revenue keeps climbing, the Bear case is wrong and the whole band should move up. If unallocated cost of revenues stays near Q2's $6.7M rather than reverting toward Q1's $23.9M, the consolidated margin is cleaner than modelled here. Conversely, a single quarter back below 45% consolidated gross margin would confirm the mix read and put the Bear case in play.

input.fundamentals_source: The FY2027 figures below are Wall Street analyst consensus estimates — the model does no forecasting of its own. Consensus is unusually split this cycle (FY2027 EPS estimates run from ~$98 to ~$150), so the forward figure is the softest, highest-impact input: change the estimate you feed in and the fair value moves directly.

input.peer_group: Scaled security platforms (CrowdStrike, Zscaler, Fortinet, Check Point)
input.peers_intro: Forward multiples for the four scaled security platforms PANW is actually compared against. Note how wide the range is: the cohort spans a no-growth incumbent to a hyper-growth cloud name, so these bracket the answer rather than set it. EV/FCF is derived as EV/Sales ÷ free-cash-flow margin, so it is on the same basis for every name.
input.figures_intro: PANW's fiscal year ends 31 July, so FY2027 is the first full year that includes CyberArk. Revenue and free cash flow are analyst consensus (51 analysts); non-GAAP EPS is derived from consensus revenue at the company's own margin targets, because consensus EPS on a GAAP basis is not comparable to the peer P/Es above. Deliberately, no GAAP earnings figure is used anywhere in this model.
input.fundamentals_source: FY2027 revenue $13.83B and adjusted free cash flow $5.25B are analyst consensus. Non-GAAP EPS $4.05 is derived, not consensus: $13.83B revenue × 30% non-GAAP operating margin (FY2026 guidance was 28.9–29.2%, with a stated long-term target in the low-to-mid 30s), plus ~$0.15B other income, taxed at PANW's 22% non-GAAP rate, over ~825M diluted shares. For context, consensus GAAP net income for the same year is only $1.53B — roughly a third of free cash flow — which is exactly why a GAAP P/E on this stock reads above 100× and carries no information.

market.commentary: Close on 13 August 2026, at an all-time high and up roughly 114% year to date. Shown here only to be explained, not to be beaten: the fair value above is computed without reference to it.

expectations.commentary: Each path takes the FY2027 revenue above, compounds it three years to FY2030, applies a free-cash-flow margin, and solves for the one number left over: the multiple PANW would still have to command in 2030 for today's price to be right. FY2030 is the horizon because it is the company's own planning horizon — management targets $20B of next-generation-security ARR by then, raised from $15B.

paths.name: Consensus-ish
paths.comment: Growth decelerating from 21% to mid-teens as the CyberArk contribution laps, at the company's stated 40% FCF margin.

paths.name: Company plan ($20B ARR)
paths.comment: Management's own FY2030 plan delivered in full: $20B NGS ARR plus legacy revenue is roughly $24B total, at the 40% margin target.

paths.name: Plan + margin upside
paths.comment: The plan delivered and cash conversion pushed five points past the target — about as good as this business plausibly gets.

input.history_intro: QuickLogic's cost of revenue is not a cost of goods. It is engineering capacity and the amortization of capitalized IP, and it sits still while revenue swings. Over the eleven quarters the company has disclosed, revenue ranged from $2.0M to $7.5M while cost of revenue stayed inside $1.5M-$3.2M; regressing one on the other gives an R-squared of 0.005. That is why the gross margin below runs from -23% to +77% without anyone at the company deciding anything about margin. In this table the breakeven revenue is simply that year's own cost base in dollars, and the gap between revenue and it is the operating result.
input.bridge_intro: No gross margin is assumed anywhere in this model. Each case names a revenue level; the cost of revenue is a fixed dollar block plus a small genuinely variable share, and the margin is whatever is left. The cost base is calibrated to the 2025-H1'26 regime, in which the company carried roughly $12.6M of annualized cost of revenue against $21M of annualized revenue.
input.figures_source: Cost base calibrated from the FY2025 and H1 2026 filed figures (10-K filed 2026-03-27; 10-Q filed 2026-08-12). At FY2026's guided revenue the calibration reproduces the company's own statement that H2 2026 would be cash-flow positive. Balance sheet at 2026-06-28: cash $18.475M, revolver $5.0M, notes payable $2.568M.

history.note: 58.5% gross margin on $12.7M of revenue - the same cost base that would later produce 22% on $13.8M.
The one year revenue cleared the cost base. EBIT +$70K on $21.2M - and the breakeven column says $21.1M, which is the whole method in one row.
Revenue fell $5.9M and cost of revenue rose $3.2M in the same year. Gross margin printed 22.0%, and Q3 printed -23.3%, without any change in what the company sells or how it prices it.

Trailing four quarters through 2026-06-28. D&A has gone from $1.0M to $5.9M in four years as capitalized IP and mask sets came on stream; most of it sits in cost of revenue, which is why the gap between the EBIT and EBITDA breakevens is now nearly $6M wide.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.comment: 2025 repeats: the government and eFPGA contracts that drove the 2026 ramp finish and the next tranche slips a year, so revenue steps back down from the ~$27M Q4'26 exit rate. EBITDA goes back below the line, the earnings multiple has nothing to bite on, and the franchise floor is the whole value. Shares carry the ATM they would have to run to fund it.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.comment: The eFPGA pipeline converts at a normal rate: +33% on FY2026's guided ~$24M, roughly +18% on the Q4'26 exit run-rate. Gross margin lands in the mid-50s purely from absorption, EBIT crosses zero for the second time in the company's history, and EBITDA reaches ~$7M. Note that the revenue floor still binds at these multiples - even in the base case this is not yet an earnings stock.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.comment: FY2026's 70-80% growth repeats once: Intel 18A and the rad-hard defense programs move from development contracts to volume, and the architectural-license model starts producing royalties. Cost base steps up to deliver it, but revenue outruns it by enough that EBITDA reaches $13.5M and the earnings multiple finally takes over from the floor.

market.commentary: At $12.63 the equity is $231M and the enterprise value $220M - against $16.3M of trailing revenue and a company that has cleared its own cost base in exactly one year out of the last ten. The two routes to that number are a 6.9x multiple on our base-case FY2027 revenue, or a 31x multiple on our base-case FY2027 EBITDA. Read as a revenue requirement, the price is asking for FY2027 revenue of about $38M - roughly the bull case, one year out, with no slippage.

action.rationale: The two inputs that decide this report are the anchor revenue level and the floor multiple, and both rest on judgment rather than filed figures: revenue is a contract pipeline whose last full year fell 30% after being guided up, and the 4.5x floor is set off a peer group (CEVA 8.4x, Arteris 16.9x, Rambus 15.6x sales) whose members are two to forty times QuickLogic's size and none of which is loss-making at this scale. The cases run $3.93 to $14.41 - a 3.7x spread - so a fraction of the weighted value would mostly be a statement about the weights. The accumulate level is therefore the bear case itself, which is the one number in the report that does not depend on the pipeline converting.
action.review: Q3 2026 revenue comes in at or above the ~$6.8M the full-year guidance implies, and the company names the FY2027 contracts behind it - or it misses, and the 2025 pattern is confirmed as the base rate rather than the exception.
